Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01641

If we look broadly at the development of Arab-Islamic thought from the earliest period of Islam all the way to what is called the “modern Arab Renaissance” of the nineteenth century, we can see the problem of predestination returning whenever Arab society faced conditions similar to those that had first brought it to the surface.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01642
But it did not always return in the same form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01643
Its form changed from one period to another according to the conditions of each age and according to the level reached by intellectual development at that time.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01644
Among the Muʿtazilites, for example, the problem appeared in a more advanced form than it had among the earliest Qadarites, especially in the logical structure of their arguments and proofs.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01645
Later, in Arab-Islamic philosophy, the same problem became connected with the universal law of causality.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01646
In Ibn Rushd, for example, this law comes close to what Marxist dialectical materialism calls the category of necessity.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01647
Yet the necessity imposed by causal law takes a metaphysical form in Ibn Rushd, while containing a materialist content within it. We will examine this when we discuss Ibn Rushd.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01648

We also find the same problem appearing among Islamic reformers such as Shaykh Muḥammad ʿAbduh at the beginning of the modern Arab “Renaissance.” There it takes a new form with an almost directly social content.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01649
The same problem was also discussed in European philosophy by Hobbes, Spinoza, Holbach, Schelling, Hegel, and later philosophical schools all the way to Marxism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01650
In Marxism, the relationship between freedom and necessity is one of the major philosophical questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01651
From a Marxist point of view, however, necessity with no place for chance leads to absolute determinism—jabr—which rules out the possibility of freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01652

What matters for us here is that throughout Arab-Islamic history there was repeatedly a need for thinkers capable of giving expression to one or both sides of the struggle between exploiting classes and groups on one side and exploited classes and groups on the other.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01653
Historically, the first of these—the exploiting classes and groups within Arab-Islamic society—repeatedly made use of Islamic religious texts whose surface meaning seemed to support predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01654
They turned these texts into a theoretical, ideological, and political weapon.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01655
With it, they defended their own existence, promoted the idea that their domination should last indefinitely, and at the same time encouraged the exploited classes and groups to submit to fate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01656
In this way, they tried to dull their revolutionary spirit, suppress their class aspirations, and weaken their willingness to struggle.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01656
The Origin of the Name “Qadarites”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01657
One final point remains about the earliest founders of the Qadarite movement: why they were called Qadarites, and why their school became known as the Qadariyya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01658
Strictly speaking, the name is inaccurate. In fact, it is the opposite of what these thinkers actually believed.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01659
The name seems to suggest that they believed human will was ruled by divine decree, whereas their position was precisely the reverse.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01660
How, then, did the name “Qadarites” become attached to them—and later to the Muʿtazilites as well?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01661

Most likely, it was their opponents, and later the opponents of the Muʿtazila, who attached the name to them as an insult and a way of discrediting them. They applied to them the saying attributed to the Prophet:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01662
“The Qadarites are the Magians of this community.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01663
The Muʿtazilites themselves rejected the name. They argued that the term Qadarites should properly be applied to those who say that divine decree, both good and evil, comes entirely from God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01664
But that belief is different from—and indeed the opposite of—the view held by the earliest “Qadarites” and by their Muʿtazilite successors, as we have already seen and will see again later.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01665
For this reason, names such as the People of Divine Unity and the People of Justice fit the Muʿtazilites better than any of the other names given to them, even the name “Muʿtazila” itself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01666
We will explain the meaning of these two names later.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01667
D — The Jabriyya, or Jahmiyya
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01668
First — A Rational Logic
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01669
The deterministic school, or the theory of jabr, holds an important place in the early history of rational thought and in the development that prepared the way for Muʿtazilite thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01670
The Jabriyya and the Qadariyya both grew from a common rational logic.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01671

The historical importance of the Jabriyya is not cancelled out by the fact that their theory was the negative opposite of human free will, or by the fact that ruling classes and social groups used it ideologically to defend and preserve their power.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01672
Those two facts remain important and cannot be ignored.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01673
But neither of them removes the major importance of the Jabriyya’s role in helping to lay the foundations of rational inquiry in the history of Arab-Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01674
The Jabriyya were also called the Jahmiyya, after Jahm ibn Ṣafwān.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01675
Al-Shahrastānī, however, treats the Jahmiyya as only one of three groups within the wider Jabriyya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01676
He first defines jabr as “denying that the human being truly performs the act and attributing it instead to the Lord.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01677
He then says that the Jabriyya fall into several groups.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01678
The pure determinists deny that human beings possess any action of their own or any power to act at all.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01679
The moderate determinists allow that human beings possess a power, but say that this power has no effect on what happens.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01680
As for those who say that the created human capacity has some effect on an action, and call this effect acquisition (kasb), al-Shahrastānī says that they should not be regarded as Jabriyya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01681

He then says that the Jahmiyya were the followers of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, who belonged to the pure deterministic group. His doctrine first appeared in Tirmidh. Salm ibn Aḥwaz al-Māzinī killed him at Marw near the end of Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01682
Second — The Theory of the Jahmiyya
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01683
Al-Shahrastānī summarizes Jahm’s position on predestination and on human power as follows:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01684

“A human being has no power over anything and cannot be described as possessing ability. He is compelled in his actions and has no power, will, or choice. God creates actions in him just as He creates what happens in all other inanimate things. Actions are attributed to the human being only figuratively, not in reality, just as actions are attributed to inanimate things. We say that a tree bore fruit, water flowed, a stone moved, the sun rose and set, the sky became cloudy and rained, and the earth shook and produced plants, and so on. Reward and punishment are also matters of compulsion, just as all actions are. Jahm said: once compulsion is established, religious obligation—the command to do something or refrain from doing it—is itself also a matter of compulsion.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01685
In this passage, Jahm appears to take the most extreme possible negative and reactionary position on human freedom of choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01686
But another statement attributed to him by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī may seem to soften this position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01687
There Jahm says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01688

“In reality, no one acts except God alone. He is the true agent. Human actions are attributed to people only figuratively, just as we say that the tree moved, the heavenly sphere turned, or the sun changed position, when in reality God caused all this in the tree, the sphere, and the sun. Human beings, however, differ in some respects from these inanimate things. God created in the human being a power through which the action occurs, and created in him a will for the action and a choice that belongs to him alone.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01689
From this second statement, the difference between human beings and inanimate things seems to lie only in the fact that humans possess something called will and choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01690

But what is the real meaning or value of this will and choice if Jahm begins by insisting that “in reality, no one acts except God alone,” that God is the true agent, and that actions are attributed to human beings only figuratively?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01691
Once that basic principle is accepted, human will and choice become almost mechanical.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01692
Every particular act of willing that arises in a human being is itself “created by God.” In that case, the one who truly wills is God, not the human being.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01693
The same applies to choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01694
So this later statement does not change our earlier judgment of Jahm’s determinism. It remains a completely negative and absolute determinism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01695
In this respect it resembles the Ashʿarite doctrine they call acquisition (kasb), which we will discuss when we come to their school.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01696
We agree with Aḥmad Amīn that this idea of “acquisition” adds nothing and changes nothing. In the end, it still comes back to predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01697
Jahm took a very different position, however, on another set of questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01698
Here he gave reason a new place in Islamic thought for his time, and used philosophical argument in several areas.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01699
In doing so, he anticipated later rationalist thinkers such as the Muʿtazilites and the scholars of kalām, and helped lay the foundations on which they would later build their intellectual system.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01700
We will now examine the main questions in which Jahm took this rational approach before them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01700
1 — The Attributes of God
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01701
On this question, Jahm gives the judgment of reason priority over the surface meaning of Qurʾanic texts.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01702
He does not simply accept their literal wording, as conservatives who insisted on the letter of the text did.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01703
Jahm denied that God has attributes separate from His essence, such as hearing, sight, will, speech, and so on.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01704
His reason was that giving these attributes to God would make God resemble human beings, and, in his view, the Creator cannot be compared with the created.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01705
Hearing, sight, life, and speech are human qualities. Some of them are also found in animals.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01706
What, then, does Jahm do with Qurʾanic passages that attribute all these qualities to God?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01707
He turns to rational interpretation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01708

Before giving this interpretation, however, he lays down a theoretical principle. In doing so, he places the first stone in what would later become a metaphysical philosophical doctrine on this subject.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01709

Here too he came before the Muʿtazilites and the scholars of kalām, placing the question firmly within rational inquiry. The Muʿtazilites and the scholars of kalām would later develop Jahm’s theory according to their own methods of reasoning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01710
Jahm’s basic position was that God is simply an essence.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01711
If this is so, then God cannot be described by any attribute that can also be applied to something else—for example, as a thing, as existing, living, knowing, or willing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01712

He may, however, be described as powerful, as the one who brings things into existence, as the one who acts, creates, gives life, and causes death, because Jahm regarded these descriptions as belonging to God alone.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
en-ref-V2-132-1
Jahm also says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01713
“God is not a thing, is not from a thing, and is not in a thing.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01714
And he says that God:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01715

“cannot be grasped by any description, nor by knowledge of any thing, nor by imagining any thing. They know God, so they claim, only by conjecture. They apply the name of divinity to Him, but do not describe Him with any quality to which divinity itself could be applied.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01716
The last sentence means that they apply the name “God” to Him, but refuse to describe Him with any quality that could itself be treated as divine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01717
From these statements attributed to Jahm, we can see that he rejects every description of God that would make Him resemble created beings.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01718
He seems to be arguing directly against the school known as the anthropomorphists, who gave God physical or sensory qualities.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01719
They were also known as the corporealists, because the physical qualities they attributed to God pictured Him as a “thing” with a material body.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01720
Because Jahm denied that God possesses the attribute of speech, he also concluded that the Qurʾan was created—that it came into existence in time and was not eternal.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01721
God, in his view, cannot literally speak because speech is a human quality.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01722
The Qurʾan, therefore, cannot be eternal divine speech.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01723
Jahm interprets Qurʾanic verses that describe God as speaking in a non-literal way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01723
For example:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01724
“And God spoke to Moses directly.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01725
Jahm interprets “spoke” here to mean that God created speech in one of His creatures, such as a prophet.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01726
Jahm therefore also preceded the Muʿtazilites in saying that the Qurʾan was created.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01727

This later became the center of a famous historical controversy and a terrible intellectual conflict, one closely associated with the Muʿtazila and one that greatly intensified the hostility between the Muʿtazilites and the Ashʿarites.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01728
We will return to this dispute, which became known in the history of Arab-Islamic thought as the ordeal over the created Qurʾan.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01728
2 — The Question of Eternity
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01729
Jahm also introduced a new idea about eternity into Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01730
Many Qurʾanic verses clearly speak of the afterlife as everlasting. For example:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01731
“It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell, remaining there forever.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
en-ref-V2-135-1
And:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01732
“Because of what they said, gardens beneath which rivers flow, remaining there forever.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01733
Despite such verses, Jahm argues:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01734

“The movements of the inhabitants of the two eternal abodes—Paradise and Hell—will come to an end. Paradise and Hell themselves will cease to exist after their inhabitants have entered them, after the people of Paradise have enjoyed its pleasures and the people of Hell have suffered its fire. For just as we cannot conceive of movements extending infinitely backward without a beginning, neither can we conceive of movements extending infinitely forward without an end.”
